I'm thrilled to be wrapping up my first week here at FurtherAI ! Insurance professionals are some of the most resilient, hard-working, customer-obsessed people I know. Our industry requires us to understand nuanced regulations, risk exposures, market shifts, and coverage details, all while being product consultants, negotiators, and sometimes even cosplaying as a therapist. So why, then, are some insurance offices still relying on outdated software, filling out ACORD forms by hand, and having to "Print" Word documents just to convert them into PDFs (iykyk)? It's clear this is becoming a pressing issue for everyday producers and executives alike. AI adoption is no longer on the horizon, it's here today. A broker who used to pump out 10 quotes a day now has the capability to pump out 10 in an hour. An underwriter no longer needs to review 50 separate property and LHR documents, they can now get a comprehensive report that tells them whether a policy is worth the risk for the carrier. AI isn't replacing producers, underwriters, claims adjusters, etc.. Licenses, regulations, and the overall need for a human touchpoint make that impossible. But the organizations winning right now are the ones using AI to empower their team members, not replace them. This is why FurtherAI's mission is personal to me. I've seen firsthand how much the insurance industry, both insurers and insureds, needs this shift. A heartfelt thank you to my Zurich Simon State Farm team. You guys know how much you mean to me, both professionally and personally. To my new team at FurtherAI, let's build 🚀 🚀 🚀

Every frontier model is close to unbeatable at writing code, because code is the cleanest training data that has ever existed. Every repository has been tagged, structured, and made public. Underwriting has none of that. Joe Schmidt IV is a Partner at Andreessen Horowitz and a board member at FurtherAI. He's a licensed insurance agent and has spent over a decade in insurance. "Code has been perfectly tagged. It's a very clean data set. When it comes down to underwriting, there's a lot of proprietary data that the models don't have access to. And when it comes down to claims, there's a lot of data that they don't have access to." That data isn't sitting in a warehouse waiting to be pointed at a model. It gets created in the insurance work itself, which is why we build on the path of existing workflows rather than around it: → Submission intake, where the risk first enters the building → Underwriting notes, where judgment gets recorded → Claims files, where the outcome finally shows up A model that has never seen how your underwriters price a risk cannot learn to price it, and the only way it ever sees that is if something is capturing the decision as it happens. Thank you Joe Schmidt and Andreessen Horowitz for the conversation. Full episode linked in comments.

VCU NSF REU Site Students Showcase Digital Forensics Research at the 26th Annual DFRWS USA Conference—and Earn a Poster Award I am pleased to share that students from the Virginia Commonwealth University NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) Site in Digital Forensics attended the 26th Annual Digital Forensics Research Conference (DFRWS USA 2026) in Arlington, Virginia, hosted by George Mason University . The REU students presented posters highlighting the research they conducted during the summer program. The participating students represented institutions across the country: Logan Altomonte — James Madison University Arya Kunisetty — University of California, Los Angeles Sasha Babic — Randolph-Macon College Cosme Boisset — Louisiana State University New Orleans Sebastian Alcibar — Virginia Commonwealth University Emirhan Kir — Rowan University Zoe McIvor — Longwood University Vaishnavi Sharma — Purdue University Sanskriti Gyawali — Virginia Commonwealth University Their projects addressed a broad range of timely digital-forensics and cybersecurity challenges, including PLC security, unmanned aerial systems, point-of-care ultrasound forensics, Starlink network behavior, passive Wi-Fi sensing, cybercrime against older adults, and explainable AI-assisted authorship analysis. Special congratulations to Arya Kunisetty , whose poster, “Forensic Attribution of Human and Autonomous Control in Unmanned Aerial Systems,” received third prize in the poster competition. His work explored whether recovered drone telemetry can distinguish autonomous flight from human control and support the forensic attribution of individual pilots. We also sincerely thank Arya’s mentors, Suramya Pokharel and Eyuphan Bulut , for their guidance, technical support, and commitment to his research. This recognition reflects Arya’s hard work as well as the valuable mentorship that helped shape the project. Congratulations to all the REU students for their hard work, professionalism, and excellent presentations. I am deeply grateful to the faculty members, postdoctoral researchers, graduate-student mentors, and collaborators who helped the students develop their research ideas, conduct rigorous experiments, prepare their posters, and confidently present their work. I am also grateful to Dr. Kemal Akkaya , Chair of the Department of Computer Science, and the VCU College of Engineering administration, including Dean Azim Eskandarian , Senior Associate Dean Gary Tepper , and Associate Dean for Research and Innovation Susan Barker , for their continued support of undergraduate research, faculty mentorship, and the NSF REU program. It was especially rewarding to see undergraduate researchers from multiple institutions engage with the international digital-forensics community, receive constructive feedback, and build connections that will support their future academic and professional development. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) .

I turned 21 in a strange, unfamiliar place last week (that place being New Jersey) Why? To attend HackPrinceton Fall 2025 Me and my teamates Yehor Ivanenko , Daniel Yi and Ruslan Akmyradov wanted to dive deeper into our exploration of LLM-powered 3D model generation, and HackPrinceton felt like the perfect place to push the idea further. We built Suzanne, a 3D modeling AI assistant that lets you create and edit models conversationally. Instead of relying on complicated CAD workflows and expensive software, you can describe or photograph what you want and watch it take shape in real time, then refine it naturally until it’s fully 3D-print-ready, all directly in the browser. Current 3D tooling has a sharp learning curve and is costly, and that reality often blocks creativity for those who are just learning, Suzanne is our accessible solution. Tech Breakdown: - MCP routing for switching between multiple LLM tasks: planning, editing, and code generation ( 5 different AI models used in total ) - OpenSCAD code generation to produce accurate, editable, parametric geometry - WebAssembly compilation for image processing and exporting STL models directly in the browser - Hunyuan image-to-model generation for shape extraction from photos/camera - WebXR visualization to preview models at real scale in AR/VR - ElevenLabs voice responses for conversational modeling feedback and audio-based editing - Three.js + React (Typescript) UI for real-time rendering, interaction, and editing tools It was quite a challenge to implement in such a short amount of time, but we pulled it off successfully, check it out: https://lnkd.in/evUSfJFK (Try out photo model creation) https://lnkd.in/eg8RkWGc Thank you to the HackPrinceton organizers, the great people I met from Dedalus Labs , Amazon , Vibe Kanban , Capital One , Anthropic , Y Combinator , and for the support from Ryan L. from Major League Hacking along with all of the other sponsors and supporters. Thrilled to announce we won Best Design at PennApps XXVI!🏆 Our winning project tackled a big question: What if we could eliminate news bias and show people what's actually happening in the world? This is exactly the problem myself, Jatin Punjabi , and Ruslan Akmyradov tackled this challenge by building noogie - a news aggregation platform that clusters stories from multiple sources to eliminate bias. noogie automatically scrapes hundreds of articles daily from major news sources. It then uses AI to analyze and group similar stories together, identifying when multiple outlets are covering the same event. Finally, it generates neutral, comprehensive headlines for each story cluster, giving users an unbiased view of what's actually happening. Under the hood, we used sentence-transformers to convert articles into embeddings, then leveraged FAISS vector indexing for efficient similarity detection and clustering. The platform integrates OpenAI's GPT-4 API to generate those neutral headlines, while the frontend visualizes story clusters as interactive nodes using D3.js. Built with TypeScript/React on the frontend and Python Flask for the backend, all powered by Supabase for scalable data storage. Huge thanks to my incredible teammates who made this all possible, especially as this was my first hackathon! Massive gratitude to the PennApps organizers, Major League Hacking , and the University of Pennsylvania for hosting the oldest collegiate-run hackathon in the world and creating such an inspiring environment for innovation. Volunteerism seems like a waste of time up until you actually do it; then you realize it isnt about who you are today- it’s more about who you will become. You never can foresee it. My parents would sign me up to volunteer and help the poor. As a teenager, I dreaded it. BUT every time I did it, the needle moved. I gradually acquited the desire for service, not from the recognition, but from the impact in the communities I served. When I was 18, I went to Caracus, Venezula, and we built homes for the homeless; wired homes so they could have power; dug wells for fresh water. We stayed with a Franciscan Priest whose life was dedicated to serving and protecting the poor. I’ve always carried that same spirit toward helping others. Perhaps its why I love mortgage and housing; we provide a pathway to safety, security and where love can abound: and that is in a home that someone owns. Fast forward to 2026, I flew to San Francisco with my 18 year old daughter Emilie, where she will fly to Thailand with a group of girls, to volunteer her time to teach English to children. What a full circle moment. This will shape her: into what? Only the Lordknows. It will be formative at a minimum; life changing at a maximum. However this influence takes shape, it will impact her work and future family; so that perhaps one day, she will be doing the same with her 18 year old. Life has a way of coming full circle; and today, it did just that.

Have you ever started reading a research paper and realized you could barely comprehend the abstract? As one of the top three finalists in the Creativity Track at the UC Berkeley AI Hackathon 2025, myself, Evan Chisholm , Sai Rithvik Kotla , Chakshan Kothakota , and Dimple Amitha Garuadapuri tried to address this issue. We believe that oftentimes there is a comprehension barrier in academic research papers that are not generally written to explain something to a novice. activity.title: I still haven't won my FPL league ever, so I've been thinking about why most free fantasy sports models eventually hit a ceiling. Nearly all of them reduce the problem to predicting player performance. But fantasy games aren’t prediction problems, they’re decision problems, and no two managers are solving the same one. This fantasy ML tool conditions the model on the manager’s constraints from the very beginning. Imagine two Fantasy Premier League managers with the exact same squad before a gameweek. One says: “Captain Haaland, don’t sell Palmer, and play a 3-5-2.” The other wants to maximize expected points. Most optimizers begin with the same underlying reasoning and only apply those preferences as filters afterward. A constraint-conditioned model treats these as fundamentally different optimization problems from the start. That changes everything: - Constraint-aware player embeddings learn player relationships based on the active constraint set. - Automated feature discovery searches for interactions that matter under the current constraints instead of assuming one global feature space. - Dynamic feature engineering learns which features should be emphasized, or even constructed, for each manager’s specific decision problem. Recent work such as LLM-FE ( https://lnkd.in/g89bT55m ) showed that feature engineering can be discovered iteratively rather than relying entirely on handcrafted rules. I’m exploring a similar idea, but instead of searching for globally useful features, the search itself is conditioned on the manager’s constraints, allowing the learned representations and features to adapt to the optimization problem being solved rather than one predictive objective. The goal isn’t just better player predictions, it’s a decision engine that adapts its reasoning to the manager instead of forcing every manager through the same optimization pipeline. Hopefully you don’t lose your fantasy league this year because your model thinks exactly like everyone else’s. Read this for more: https://lnkd.in/gCSY_-VW . We keep making models smarter, but we haven't completely solved context. Every assistant has its own version of you. ChatGPT remembers one set of conversations. Claude remembers another. Cursor knows what happened in your codebase but not your goals. None of them share context, and none of them reliably understand what you're focused on this week. The result is strange. Your AI can help you solve really hard technical tasks, but it still asks you to explain your project pivot for the tenth time. I don't think context should belong to the model, it should belong to the user. So, I spun up Cortex. Cortex is a local-first context layer that sits above AI models. It continuously builds an evolving understanding of your long-term identity and your short-term context (projects, priorities, goals, workflows, and preferences) and makes that available to whichever assistant you're using. Instead of every model maintaining its own incomplete memory, your context becomes portable. Switch models. Start a new conversation. Try a new AI product → Your context comes with you. Inspired by Anthropic's Workspace research ( https://lnkd.in/gWzsB5pb ), Cortex extends the idea of a J-space beyond a single model. Instead of each AI building its own partial understanding of you, they all reference the same evolving workspace of your projects, goals, and preferences - similar to how a model's J-space acts as a shared workspace for the concepts it is actively reasoning about. Still early (only two integrations), but I'm excited to see where this goes and what tools I'll add in the future. I'd love feedback. Your planner doesn’t know where your project actually is. Every software project starts with a roadmap. A week later, the roadmap is already outdated. You’ve rewritten architecture, discovered new problems, abandoned features, and changed priorities, but your planner still reasons from the original plan. While watching YC's Paper Club series, I came across Scaling Self-Play with Self-Guidance ( Luke Bailey , https://lnkd.in/eWrkCxjD ), which showed how a small model outperformed a 100x larger model in trajectory-based development using asymmetric self-play instead of symmetric self-play. One idea stuck with me: instead of blindly generating the next step, generate several candidates and have a second model judge which one best advances the current state. I wondered if software planning has the same problem, so I built Frontier. Instead of planning from the end goal, Frontier reconstructs where your project actually is. It analyzes your GitHub repository (commit history, file changes, README, issues, and recent development trajectory) to infer the current frontier of the project. It then generates multiple candidate next tasks and scores them before recommending the single highest-leverage thing to work on next. To evaluate the idea, I compared Frontier against a baseline planner that only receives the project goal and deadline. Across simulated planning trajectories... - Frontier maintained substantially higher task alignment - Accumulated significantly more planning reward See a longer description and demo here: https://lnkd.in/eSjn7emn . The biggest improvements I saw using it came from recommending tasks that better matched the current trajectory of development, unblocked future work, and maintained momentum. This is still an early prototype, but I'd love feedback. My code lives at https://lnkd.in/eT9swAds . Some insights from testing are attached. ...more

I’ve noticed something strange about people who end up building interesting things. Early on, they sound a little delusional. Not loud or arrogant. Usually pretty calm. But they’ll say things that don’t quite match reality yet. They’ll talk about the company they’re building when it’s just three people and a prototype. They’ll assume they can get meetings with people far above their level. They’ll make plans that seem a bit too big for where they currently are. If you’re standing next to them, it can feel slightly uncomfortable. Like they’re getting ahead of themselves. And maybe they are. But over time I realized something. -------------- The people who sound the most “realistic” rarely start anything difficult. They wait until the path looks obvious. Until the odds make sense. Until they feel qualified. By that point, the interesting opportunities are usually gone. The people who start things earlier seem to operate differently. They assume things might work before there’s much evidence. Which sounds like delusion. -------------- But there’s a second part you notice if you watch them long enough. They’re extremely disciplined. They keep showing up long after the idea stops feeling exciting. They keep fixing things that break. They keep pushing through the awkward early phase where nothing really works yet. The delusion is what lets them start. The discipline is what keeps them going long enough for reality to slowly catch up. Most people try to choose one. They either stay realistic, or they dream. The people who end up building amazing things somehow do both. So if you’re going to be wrong about something, you might as well be wrong in the optimistic direction. Be delusional enough to believe it will work. Then disciplined enough to make sure it does. ...more ...more

Today, we’re announcing Naïve has raised a $28.5 million Series A to build autonomous company infrastructure. This round was led by Nexus, with participation from Y Combinator, Zetta, Liquid 2, and more. Dennis Zax & I have been building together since we were 14. We sold our first company as teenagers, dropped out of Berkeley, joined Y Combinator, and spent the last several years thinking about what the world looks like when agents can fully run businesses. Coding agents can now ship an app in an afternoon. But turning that app into a real operating business still takes months. Developers manually stitch together payments, incorporation, email, phone numbers, compute, memory, databases, authentication, and dozens of other services — infra built for human operators, not autonomous agents. Naïve is rebuilding and unifying the entire business stack for agents. Today, thousands of developers write a single config file, and Naïve provisions everything their agents need behind one API: > Real-world Identity: KYC/KYB, LLC formation, Email, Phone, Virtual Cards > Cloud: Database, Hosting, Compute, Storage, Auth > Serverless Agents: Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, Vetta > Orchestration: Task Management, Interagent Communication, Scheduling > Inference / Model Routing > Memory: One context layer that grows with the entire company. > 10k+ Tool Gateway: Stripe, Github, Quickbooks, Higgsfield, Browser, etc. > Governance: Enforce capability policies, audit logs, HITL approval With this new capital, we’re investing deeply into our new lab with four research areas: serverless agents, inference, brain, and agent workforce orchestration. Our early benchmarks can start an agent in 2.3 milliseconds using 1.2MB, reduce inference costs several-fold, and achieve stronger memory recall with 11x fewer tokens per query. In this next decade, agent spend is set to scale into the trillions as companies completely run on agents that finish work autonomously. Our vision with our research is to make each token do more, so autonomous companies can become a cost-efficient reality. Went down a rabbit hole on what happens when one AI agent fails. Built ForkLab around it solo & won Best Use of Braintrust at Daytona HackSprint. ForkLab tests recovery policies by replaying the same distributed-system failure across eight isolated environments. Agentic LLM loop optimization has been everywhere this past week, so I built a fully open-source correctness oracle that catches a model cheating to look faster than it is... Here's everything you need to know: Tools like Google DeepMind 's AlphaEvolve and its open-source version, OpenEvolve, optimize code in a loop: a model proposes a faster version, a scorer grades it, the best ones survive, and repeat. The recent ComPilot paper validated how well this works when an off-the-shelf LLM is paired with a compiler that checks every change is legal and actually faster. The catch is that the loop is only as honest as its scorer. Give a model a naive scorer, and it stops optimizing and starts cheating. It returns code that looks 100x faster, but quietly memorizes your test inputs... so it's wrong on everything else, and the loop rewards it anyway. Tripwire is the scorer that catches it. It's an easy-to-use CLI that drops into the loop and re-runs every "optimized" version on fresh adversarial inputs the model never saw. A cheat passes the visible tests and dies on the hidden ones. TL;DR: Don't trust the loop to be correct... use a proper verification layer for correctness. Fully open source, MIT, and free to use right now. This past spring, I presented a poster at UC Riverside's Undergraduate Research Symposium on multimodal RAG over 5G specifications. It was the end of about a year of work: finding the problem, learning the fundamentals, building the thing, then rebuilding the parts I got wrong. 5G specs run thousands of pages, dense with diagrams and tables. I built a retrieval pipeline over them and tested what actually works on documentation that dense. The main comparison was between two ways of handling figures. One embeds images and text together in a single shared space. The other has a vision model describe every figure in plain text, then embeds only that. The whole thing runs on open weights in the 3 to 4 billion parameter range, locally with Ristretto-3B doing the figure descriptions, nomic-embed-text and CLIP as the two embedding paths, and Qwen and Gemma as base models, served through Ollama and Weaviate in Docker. I used small models deliberately so the results reflect the retrieval pipeline, not the raw strength of a frontier model. Scored against the ORAN-Bench-13K benchmark, the text-grounded approach won clearly. For specs this text-heavy, cross-modal comparison mostly introduces noise. Keyword search also carried more weight than I expected, and the two embedding types responded to query blending in opposite directions, which points to dynamic tuning per query. I'm continuing this work in the lab, in two directions. First, better evaluation: multiple-choice accuracy only tells you a system picked the right answer, not whether it actually understood the spec, so I'm looking at stronger evaluation strategies. Second, agentic capabilities: moving past answering questions about the spec toward actually applying it, using what the pipeline retrieves to reason about real codebases and real deployment scenarios. A poster makes a year look a lot more linear than it was. Funded and guided by the UCR Chancellor's Research Fellowship , with thanks to my PI, Dr. Zhaowei Tan .

publications.title: Generating Post-Acetazolamide Cerebral Blood Flow MRI for High-risk Stroke Patients
publications.subtitle: Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (MIDL)
publications.description: (First Author; presenting at MIDL 2026 Taiwan) Abstract: Cerebrovascular reserve (CVR) quantifies the brain’s ability to augment cerebral blood flow in response to a vasodilatory stimulus and is a key biomarker in Moyamoya disease and other steno-occlusive cerebrovascular disorders. Clinically, CVR is typically assessed by administering acetazolamide (ACZ) and acquiring post-ACZ perfusion maps, but this workflow is time-consuming, costly, and contraindicated in a subset of patients. In this work, we investigate whether deep learning can predict post-ACZ perfusion directly from baseline arterial spin labeling (ASL) MRI, enabling pharmacological-free CVR estimation. We curate a single-center dataset of Moyamoya ASL perfusion imaging, comprising pre/post-ACZ scan pairs from 194 patients. We design a post-ACZ conditional Autoencoder (cAE) network to regress the middle axial post-ACZ slice from the corresponding pre-ACZ slice using a combined L1 and SSIM loss. We evaluate our method against three diffusion-based formulations (conditional DDPM, Cold Diffusion, and Residual Diffusion). On a hold-out test set of 49 patients, the proposed post-ACZ cAE achieves the highest reconstruction fidelity (SSIM ≈0.79), outperforming diffusion-based baselines in MAE, SSIM, and PSNR. Region-wise analysis of CBF percentage change in affected versus healthy MCA territories showed that the generated post-ACZ model outputs followed ground truth patterns of cerebrovascular reserve. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of non-invasive CVR assessment using MRI for high-risk patients. Our data-driven approach could reduce reliance on ACZ challenges in routine clinical workflow and expand access to CVR testing to evaluate brain health.

patents.description: ControLearn SDBT is an interactive sensory development bubble tube to be used for the relaxation and sensory development of children/individuals with developmental disorders (such as Autism, ADHD, etc.). It allows for the creation and control of different light environments, as well as control of the speed at which bubbles are released, which suits various requirements of different individuals using ControLearn SDBT, as well as psychologists using it to administer therapy in a controlled multisensory environment (snoezelen room). By watching bubbles rise in the tube and feeling the vibrations the air pump produces, children/individuals with developmental disorders can improve their visual and tactile senses, and also their attention and concentration capabilities. Furthermore, the ability to control the device through buttons helps improve motor skills, as it teaches control through switch use. Individuals are thus able to eventually perform more complex motor tasks.

My first ever funded flight was when I led a contingent to represent IISER Tirupati for Entrepreneurial Summit 2025 at IISER KOLKATA along with my senior Pratik Kumar Panda 18 years old. Leading a contingent of 10 . No prior experience. The night before the pitch event, we did something that changed the outcome. We scrapped our approach. Not the idea. The framing. We researched our judges , their backgrounds, what they'd built, what they valued. New data. New hypothesis. We iterated the entire presentation overnight. Same product. Completely reframed for the specific humans in the room. One of our teams won second place . This is exactly what physics teaches you — you don't commit to a hypothesis forever. When new information arrives, you update and move fast. Most pitches fail not because the idea is weak. They fail because the presenter never updated their hypothesis about who they were sitting across from. The best pitch isn't the most polished one. It's the most calibrated one.

Over my summer break, I found myself, curious, severely underqualified and wide-eyed at a summer school nestled in the foothills of the Himalayas. I was one of the few undergrads in a cohort full of Physics and Math PhDs across the world attending the Summer School on Dynamical and Complexity Systems at UPES , Dehradun. Together, we gathered to explore and learn the idiosyncrasies of chaos, complexity and fractals. Not just in the lecture halls and labs, but in the cadence of our days. Surrounded by cool mist, unpredictable rainfalls and beautifully tricky mathematical equations, the days blurred into whiteboard scribbles and chai breaks, bifurcations and bus rides to Dehradun's Paltan Bazaar. Between these lectures and trips to the city, I began to feel something rare, something that I never expected in a summer school: belonging. I was fortunate to find people who would accompany me for late night walks, badminton sessions and impromptu snack breaks. Making use of the knowledge I learned throughout the labs and lectures, I presented an early-stage research idea at the intersection of nonlinear dynamics and neuroscience, proposing novel ways to model neurodivergence through the language of oscillatory systems. But beyond the academic high, this experience left me soft in the best way. There is something poetic about learning math in the mountains. Something unquantifiable about find your people among strangers. I am grateful, inspired, and more certain than ever that I want to build a life at the edge—where science meets soul, where structure flirts with spontaneity. And for making this school possible, my immeasurable thanks goes to: UPES School of Computer Science , Dr. Vinod Patidar , Manish Shrimali , Ram Ramaswamy , Vijaysekhar Chellaboina , Rām Sharma, PhD , Indian National Science Academy - INSA and many more...

I’m dropping out of Berkeley. Before you judge me, let me explain. This past semester nearly broke me. I burned out not once, but twice. I was taking five classes and trying to do everything “the right way” attending every lecture, lab, and discussion. I studied every single day and night. After classes, I’d hunt for empty lecture halls or lounge seats just to keep studying until 9 or 10 pm. Weekends weren’t breaks, they were catch-up days. On top of that, I was juggling clubs, extracurriculars, ambassador roles, networking events, mixers, socials, and trying to build real connections. Even the fun stuff took time and energy. And somehow, I still tried to show up for my friends the people who’ve supported me through everything. This isn’t a flex. It’s just the reality of trying to do everything you care about at once. It’s hard. Now I’m on winter break. Yesterday, I was back home in Florida at an arcade with my hometown friends. We laughed, yapped, smiled, and acted like nothing had changed. And for the first time in a while, my body and mind felt… calm. I realized how much I missed that feeling and how important it is to savor it. So no, I’m not actually dropping out of Berkeley. But I am dropping the lie that grinding 24/7 makes you successful. If you don’t rest, your body will force you to. Burnout isn’t a badge of honor. It’s a warning sign. You don’t need to disappear to be impressive. Take breaks. Touch grass. Protect your mind. It’s survival. And honestly? It might be the reason you don’t give up entirely. Take care of yourself. You deserve it. 💛 Comment "BREAK" if you also need to take a break and a chill pill😤✊️ #mindset #studentlife #selfcare #WorkLifeBalance

We applied to 4 accelerators: Y Combinator, 500 Global, Plug and Play, and Berkeley SkyDeck. Before that I went through 30+ programs worldwide. For roughly the same 12 weeks, you can pay 0% equity or 12%. Almost nobody compares them properly. Here are the 10 worth a founder's time. 1. Y Combinator (SF Bay Area) $125K for 7%, plus $375K on an uncapped MFN SAFE. No fees. 3 months. Outcome: Demo Day in front of the most active seed investors alive. The brand reprices your round. 2. a16z Speedrun (San Francisco) $500K for 10%, plus $500K in your next round within 18 months. $8M+ in credits, no board seat. 12 weeks, 60-70 teams, twice a year. Outcome: a16z as your first investor. 3. HF0 (San Francisco) Reported at $1M for 5%. 12 weeks, live-in. Outcome: ~10 teams per cohort, mostly repeat founders. Best terms on this list if you get in. 4. South Park Commons (SF, NYC, Bangalore) $400K for 7% now, plus $600K guaranteed at your next round. 8-week bootcamp, then open-ended residency. Outcome: built for the -1 to 0 stage, before you know what you're building. 5. Sequoia Arc (Americas and Europe) A 4-day intensive, ~10 companies. Terms are company-specific and not published. Outcome: Sequoia partners engaged pre-seed. Shortest program here by a wide margin. 6. Techstars (30+ cities worldwide) $220K: $20K for 5% common, plus $200K uncapped MFN SAFE. No fee. 3 months. APAC programs run $100K instead. Outcome: mentor-driven, but quality varies enormously by city. Pick the MD, not the logo. 7. 500 Global (Global) $150K for ~6% (negotiable). 4 months. Outcome: the most distribution-focused curriculum of the large programs. 2,500+ companies backed. 8. Entrepreneur First (London, San Francisco, Bangalore) Equity-free grant while you're still ideating, then up to $250K once you incorporate. Equity not published. Outcome: they back you before you have a co-founder or an idea. Nobody else does this at scale. 9. Berkeley SkyDeck (Berkeley, plus a Milan track) $200K for 7.5%. 6 months. 20-25 teams per batch. Outcome: strong Demo Day plus Berkeley's talent pipeline. Catch: one founder must be UC-affiliated or an international founder. 10. Plug and Play (Global) The program is equity-free. Investment is separate and optional. Outcome: Fortune 500 pilots, not investor intros. 80+ vertical programs a year. Also strong: Antler (30 cities, terms vary), EWOR (up to €500K, Europe), Alchemist (enterprise). Equity turns out to be the wrong thing to optimize. Plug and Play takes 0% and gets you corporate pilots. YC takes 7% and gets you a seed round at several times the price you'd raise alone. Both are right, for different companies. I think one of the biggest limitations of today’s AI is that its assumptions about how work gets done are already outdated. Ask it to plan a project and it’ll often estimate six months because that’s what software development looked like in the world it learned from. The problem isn’t the timeline. It’s that every recommendation that follows is conditioned on that assumption. What should you build? Which architecture should you choose? What should you prioritize? Those decisions all depend on how expensive the model believes software development is. Simply retraining on newer data probably won’t fully solve this. Training data teaches models how work was done, not how work changes when AI is doing a significant fraction of it. I think future AI systems will need to continuously update their priors as AI changes the nature of work itself. Otherwise they’ll keep optimizing for constraints that no longer exist.

There is a short clip doing the rounds from Jeff Bezos that genuinely stayed with me. It comes from Tim Dodd’s exclusive tour of Blue Origin’s New Glenn factory in Cape Canaveral, Florida. What stood out was not the scale of the rocket. Bezos walks through the facility, closely observing how teams work on New Glenn. He points out details most leaders would skip. The GS1 booster’s aft section with seven BE-4 engines. The midsection tanks. The forward section. The second-stage hydrogen tank. But the real moment is his interaction with employees. He listens. He asks questions. He looks genuinely curious, not performative. I strongly resonate with this. Because leadership is not about walking the floor to be seen. It is about walking the floor to understand. The best leaders I have learned from share one habit. They stay close to the work. Not to micromanage. But to respect the people doing it. When leaders understand the details, teams feel valued. When teams feel valued, quality improves. And when quality improves, speed and innovation follow naturally. This clip is a reminder. Vision matters. But presence matters more. #leadership #amazon #workculture #jeffbezos

Today, I am excited to share that Bunkerhill Health has raised $55 million from Vinod Khosla at Khosla Ventures , Alfred Lin from Sequoia Capital , Y Combinator , and other amazing investors. Our mission is to make it radically easy for health systems to turn their ideas into reality through AI agents—improving patient outcomes, bending the cost curve, and making healthcare operations dramatically more efficient. The University of Texas Medical Branch is running 20+ AI agents - live - across the enterprise on Bunkerhill. One of those agents - in its first month - flagged a patient at imminent risk of heart attack, leading to a life-saving open heart surgery. Another one, a nephrology triage agent, cut wait times for appointments by >50%. Yet another one, a lung nodule agent, addressed urgent cases 80% faster and doubled guideline-concordant follow-ups. That is what Peter McCaffrey, MD, calls Bunkerhill: “a shared brain” for the health system. That’s the promise of AI finally being realized in healthcare. Making it possible requires two things: (1) a shared layer of intelligence for the entire health system, and (2) an operating model to enable rapid development of AI agents for the problems they understand best. Together, these dramatically reduce the cost and time required to turn an idea into a working solution. As that cost approaches zero, the limiting factor is no longer technology. It is imagination—and the conviction to act. The health systems we work with have both. Our job is to make sure nothing else stands in their way.

Last month, I officially graduated from Stanford University with a Master's in Civil and Environmental Engineering, with a focus on sustainable urban systems. Over the past month, I have been reflecting on how much this experience changed me. When I arrived at Stanford, I knew that I wanted to build a career focused on sustainability in infrastructure, but I did not yet know exactly what that could look like. I am leaving with a much clearer understanding of the many ways sustainability can manifest in infrastructure systems, thanks to opportunities to learn by doing, such as: • spending a summer in New York City working with the Built Ecology team at WSP and learning about decarbonization across different scales of the built environment. • travelling to the UK for a week-long Sustainability Changemakers course at the University of Oxford , where I learned how leaders in finance, journalism, policy, and other fields are advancing greener outcomes. • working as a Research Assistant with Dr. Khalid Osman at the Osman Lab, where I studied access to water infrastructure through community-based participatory research. This experience of collaborating with community-based organizations completely changed how I think about infrastructure, showing me that the people using these systems should be at the center of their design. • serving as a Living Lab Fellow at Sustainable Stanford , helping shape Stanford's approach to measuring and reducing embodied carbon by evaluating next-generation tools and informing university policy under the mentorship of Samantha Lubow and David Kirk . It showed me how research, policy, and data can come together to inform real decisions and create impact beyond a single project. More than anything, I am grateful for the professors, mentors, colleagues, and best friends I met at Stanford. They challenged me, supported me, and inspired me every day. Stanford and everything I learned there have changed the way I think about impact, opportunity, and responsibility. I am also excited to share that I joined the Environmental Defense Fund last week as a Lokey Fellow working on clean electricity and markets. I am deeply grateful to Alex DeGolia and the Haas Center For Public Service for making this opportunity possible. This feels like the perfect way to begin my career: working at an organization with a long history of creating meaningful environmental impact and applying the lessons Stanford taught me about combining technical knowledge, policy, collaboration, and public service. I have been incredibly fortunate to have opportunities and privileges that very few receive. I hope to use them responsibly and contribute to a more equitable world with clean air, energy, and water for all.

At some point, its pace is bound to slow, stagnate, or even regress. While this may seem pessimistic, the causes of such a plateau are not necessarily mysterious. In this paper, I propose that the primary limiting factor of a society is individual selfish behaviour: specifically, the unwillingness of individuals to share transformative discoveries or technologies with the wider population. Importantly, I argue that this pattern is not only observable in real history but also logically deducible through basic thought experiments. I further suggest that although selfishness is deeply rooted, this barrier can be consciously recognized and corrected.

activity.title: 865 endpoints. 800 PRs. 4 weeks. Clayton Winders just published how agents migrated Clipboard's APIs to strict contract validation without disrupting production traffic. These were the endpoints we least wanted to touch: years of partial data migrations, dead experiments, and database internals leaking through. A single "convert this to strict types, make no mistakes" prompt wasn't going to cut it. Neither was a multi-thousand-line PR no one wanted to review. I've written that our thesis is verification over generation. Clayton's post shows what that looks like in practice: 𝗗𝗿𝘆-𝗿𝘂𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁. A NestJS middleware validates every response against a best-approximation contract and logs mismatches instead of failing requests. There's no better validator than production traffic. 𝗙𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹. ~300 endpoints logged contract mismatches despite passing typechecking. Agents triaged the warning logs with an agent skill, encoded the common failure modes, then opened fix PRs. 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗯𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻. One agent per endpoint produces conflicting changes to shared schemas. One agent for all 865 blows the context window; the contract package alone tokenizes to ~450K tokens. ~40 batches, farmed out by 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘄 ( https://lnkd.in/geN5-R4h ), hit the sweet spot. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲. Silence isn't success. An endpoint only graduates from dry-run to strict after serving real traffic with zero warnings. "The agents don't need to be right the first time, they need a way to be told when they're wrong." Full post: https://lnkd.in/gJWwudzz We're hiring engineers who want to build this way: https://lnkd.in/g78Merj4 ...more ...more

The loudest critic of my last post, "with 30 minutes left in my day, I queue tickets, close the lid, and wake up to PRs," said I must be "rubber-stamping slop." He's half right. He's right that no one can meaningfully review 50 substantial pull requests a day. He's wrong about what's in those PRs and underestimates how good agent code gets with the right guardrails. Most tickets aren't features. They're the mundane or forever-backlog work: — Flaky test fixes. Run the candidate fix 50 times in CI; green means it's low-risk to merge. — Dependabot updates that fail CI. Agents triage, fix, or close. — Stale feature flags at 100% rollout. Agents delete the dead branches. — The long tail of a 1M-line JavaScript-to-TypeScript migration. Each one is scoped, with a tight feedback loop where review is cheap. The PR volume is a side effect of clearing that backlog, not a target. What makes it safe to let these run overnight is the harness around the model. I wrote up the rest: How tickets route, what fits, and what doesn't yet. The tools that power it are open-source: https://lnkd.in/gyw3hy2F Thanks to Clayton Winders , who built the initial version. Can we all agree that we may be holding too low of expectations for the recruiting industry? While that's great to hear, in what other world is 21% considered a "good" percentage? ➡️ Our team has been making a concerted effort to give some more specific feedback to candidates, especially when they're rejected at later stages. Hey, you've spent a lot of time with us on a case study and a few live interviews, the least we can do is give a brief summary of why we didn't select you. In ramping this up it has been ASTOUNDING how many candidates reply with some version of, "I'm disappointed, but thank you for the feedback, it's so rare to get any insight on why I was rejected!" I say all of this with an acute awareness that our team at Clipboard has certainly been part of the problem at times, and still has a long way to go. Neuramill was selected for the Seattle Tech Week Showcase, and I realized one of the biggest challenges of pitching a software-first deep tech company. It was convincing people that a software-first company can be solving one of the hardest deep-tech problems. We’ve become so good at building software for the digital world that we’re almost wired to assume software is a solved category. Deep tech, on the other hand, makes people think of rockets, robots, satellites, or new materials. But one of the hardest unsolved problems is that software doesn’t naturally understand the physical world. And yet those rockets, robots, drones, and factories all rely on software to interact with it. A machinist can hear a cut, see a tool vibrate, recognize a setup, and instantly know what should happen next. A computer or a machine can’t. Someone has to translate decades of physical intuition into something machines can reason about. In manufacturing, that bridge has traditionally been experienced machinists and programmers. Many of them are retiring. Our job is to build the software bridge that captures that knowledge so the next generation can go from a 3D design to an executable process with far less friction and ultimately build the physical things our world depends on, faster. One lesson the technical side of my brain keeps relearning when pitching is that : “$30 trillion physical market” might be the fact but start with what your audience already experiences and cares about. The aircrafts. The rockets. The robots. The autonomous drones. The machines that feel like they’re straight out of Tony Stark’s workshop, Transformers, or WALL·E. That’s the future people imagine. Then show them the invisible software that makes that future possible. Sometimes the hardest part of building deep tech is painting a simple dotted line to your well researched, data driven vision. It’s helping people see that the most transformative technology that will change their lives is often the least noticed one. Thank you to J.P. Morgan and team for organizing such a fun showcase.

A machine shop’s solution to a million dollar problem: egg cartons. Egg cartons have been used in manufacturing since the mid 20th century. Today, they protect high tolerance parts from collisions, friction, and the smallest defects during transport. Sometimes the most elegant engineering solution isn't engineered at all. To me, egg cartons represent something larger. They are a reminder that the best solutions often come from unexpected places. That progress happens when ideas, and people, from different worlds collide. Sometimes the thing that looks completely out of place is exactly what's needed. The way I experience manufacturing is dynamic, multidimensional, and yet somehow incredibly precise and still. I was drawn to data science, and eventually machine learning and AI, because I was fascinated by the idea of taking millions of signals, letting them interact, and uncovering patterns hidden inside the chaos. Analyzing, predicting, and understanding the world through complexity. Now, I feel the exact same part of my brain light up in a machine shop. There is a quiet choreography between a dozen pieces of metal: the workpiece, the fixture, the cutting tool, the stock, the vise. Every interaction is intentional. The tool must engage the workpiece, but never the fixture. The sound matters. The clean pitch, the chatter that tells you something is wrong. Every operation is planned, yet a thousandth of an inch can change the entire outcome. Delicate parts with impossibly thin walls, held to tolerances measured in thousandths, are gently placed into egg cartons before beginning their journey into a $16 trillion industry. A world that doesn't just run on 0s and 1s, but on atoms and bits, where physical reality demands the same unconventional thinking that vectors once demanded from me in multidimensional space.

We won the last 250 years. We invented, built, and learnt. Manufacturing is the foundation of this country. We must continue to invent, build, and preserve the hard-won knowledge. Neuramill is building the intelligence layer for American manufacturing to win the next 250. 🇺🇸

Please welcome Saina Deshpande to Neuramill as a Software Engineering Intern, joining us from Massachusetts Institute of Technology ! At Neuramill , we're building physical AI for high-precision manufacturing, turning engineering intent into manufacturable decisions. Excited to have Saina on the team. What excites you about manufacturing and AI? When Sonnet 4.5 was released back in 2025, we saw the model exhibit a behavior that came to be known as "context anxiety": as it approached its context window limit, it would wrap work up early and stop with room to spare. To compensate for this behavior, we spent time and energy building in context resets into our agent harnesses. But when Opus 4.5 shipped, the model stopped showing this behavior entirely, so the harness fixes we built in turned into pure overhead. Harnesses encodes assumptions about what the model cannot do on its own today, and those assumptions go stale as models improve. Check out our talk that Gagan Bhat and I gave at AI Engineer World's Fair, where we discuss the lessons we learned building harnesses that adapt alongside models: https://lnkd.in/gdX4xbXt Huge shoutout to AI Engineer for hosting an amazing conference - what a fun crowd to present to!

GutGutGoose (YC S26) makes personalized probiotics that engineer the human microbiome. Personalization is the future of healthcare, yet the entire probiotics industry is still operating under a one-size-fits-all premise. The formulations are made without knowing anything about the individual consuming them. Everyone gets the same bacterial strains, the same dosage, and when nothing works, the customer is left to make another guess. They’ve eliminated the guessing by customizing the pill to every single person. Customers send in a stool sample, giving our testing facilities over 5GB of extensive microbiome data. An algorithm uses that data to create a digitized clone of the microbiome, test thousands of bacterial strains against it, and find ones that will colonize and be of benefit. These strains are then compiled into a supply of probiotics. Every 3 months, they test again to see how the microbiome has changed, and use the results to improve the next formula. The longitudinal gut data collected will be used in the future to be able to identify chronic diseases such as Alzheimer’s and dementia, years before they begin to affect the individual. We hosted the official YC afterparty for Startup School this year. More than 1000 people registered, but we could only fit about 200 in the room. After a day that big and that packed, we wanted something low-key. So we got a venue by the water, a DJ, and a couple hundred builders who wanted to keep the conversations going without the conference-hall energy. Spent four hours chit-chatting with students, developers, and future founders without any agenda. It's genuinely one of the best ways to meet the next wave of people building amazing things. Two years ago, we were the ones showing up to someone else's afterparty, asking founders for advice. Hosting our own this year felt like closing a loop. The reason afterparties are such big hits is that some of the most memorable conversations from events like this happen only after everyone's decompressed a bit.
